newsitem.title: UK: WORLDMARKETS - Gold set for further punishment after slide.
newsitem.headline: WORLDMARKETS - Gold set for further punishment after slide.

text.p: Gold seems set for further punishment in 1997 after a price slide of 3-1/2 percent in the first few trading days, bullion analysts say.

Investors and consumers don't want to touch it. Producers are panicking about getting a decent return on it. And speculators are selling gold which they don't own in the hope of buying it back cheaper later.
Bullion was trading at around $355 an ounce on Thursday, down nearly $15 since the start of the new year, and few bullion dealers or analysts think its tumble is over.
"Historically, the first few days of a new year have set the tone for the first quarter. So it looks like weakness is set to continue," said one senior London bullion dealer.
At the very least, most say, gold prices look poised to crumble in the next few weeks to the psychological $350 to $345 area, an important historic low from 1993.
Beyond that, $325 is a realistic target in the next few months, said technical analyst Cliff Green of Trend Analysis.
"The acceleration and speed we have seen last week is something we haven't seen for a long time," Green said.
Where the slide will halt will depend on when gold starts looking cheap enough to start buying again, analysts said.
Buoyant stock and bond markets and steady U.S. inflation, the roots of gold's decline in recent months, continue to discourage investors from putting money into bullion.
Prices have been trending lower since hitting a five-year high of $417 last February.

But a break below $370 late last year took prices to a level not seen for three years. It also released gold from a price "stranglehold", ranging roughly between $370 and $390, created by holders and issuers of options, analysts say.

"Below $370 we're in new territory, so things are open to a lot more volatility," said metals market analyst Tony Warwick-Ching of CRU International, who forecasts a near-term trading range of $345 to $360.
Meanwhile, big investment funds, mostly U.S.-based, have been selling the market "short" in force, in anticipation of taking a profit if prices sink still lower.
Gold producers, particularly in Australia, are also growing increasingly anxious to lock in prices for future output before values decline further, analysts say.
And overshadowing these market woes is concern that European central banks will sell some of their large gold reserves this year in order to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
"The actual impact of real identifiable central bank sales has been modest," Warwick-Ching said. "But it has made investors and consumers very wary and the result has been this erosion."
The World Gold Council, a promotional body for the gold mining industry, said that worldwide demand for gold remained strong in the fourth quarter despite the price slide.

But the demand has failed to make a noticeable impact on the recent price fall. Analysts say price-sensitive consumers are likely to put off buying gold until they are convinced that prices have hit bottom.
Japanese industry sources on Thursday said gold demand in Japan was seen easing further this year from already depressed levels in 1996.
